title: Mac and Dennis Become EMTs

jokes.text: The gang rattles off medical jargon over a dying man while simultaneously covering up their own role in his cardiac arrest
jokes.setup: Two voices alternate between competent-sounding EMT terminology ('OPA,' 'purple cyanosis,' 'diaphoretic') and panicked deflection
jokes.punchline: The medical jargon is immediately undercut by 'We've never seen him before at all. He's a total outsider' — their cover story bleeding into their emergency response
jokes.explanation: Smart cold open structure: the interweaving of real medical terms with panicked alibi-building in the same breath is a great joke about these characters' inability to prioritize correctly. The two registers crashing together is the comedy — they can't separate 'save this man' from 'protect ourselves.'

dialogue.line: Don't think this guy's gonna make it. You hear me? Did you have an OPA. Breathing's irregular and weak.

jokes.text: 'His goddamn heart just stopped for no reason.' / 'Not no reason. You gave him a hot pepper.' / 'Don't... They don't have to know that.'
jokes.setup: Someone states the man's heart stopped 'for no reason'
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately corrects that — the ghost pepper — and Dennis hisses they shouldn't say that in front of the paramedics
jokes.explanation: Tight, fast, well-constructed. Dennis's 'They don't have to know that' is a perfect encapsulation of his pathological self-interest — the man is dying and Dennis is already in cover-up mode. Good economy, strong character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We don't know this guy from Adam. We've never seen him before at all. He's a total outsider.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I never saw him before in the bar at all.

jokes.text: 'We've never seen him before at all. He's a total outsider. I never saw him before in the bar at all.'
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to distance themselves from responsibility for the man's heart attack
jokes.punchline: They protest so much and so specifically that it's obvious they know exactly who he is and are lying badly
jokes.explanation: Classic comedy of over-protestation. The escalating denial ('total outsider', 'I never saw him before in the bar at all') works because each additional disclaimer makes them more obviously guilty. Good economy through repetition with diminishing returns used deliberately.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I thought he was, like, a jazzman. I mean, he had a ponytail. He had a piano-key tie.

jokes.text: 'I thought he was, like, a jazzman. I mean, he had a ponytail. He had a piano-key tie.'
jokes.setup: The gang is asked who the victim was
jokes.punchline: Charlie's identifying criteria are purely aesthetic — a ponytail and a piano-key tie — delivered with complete sincerity as if this explains everything
jokes.explanation: Very Charlie. His logic is internally consistent and completely absurd. 'Piano-key tie' as a defining detail is a great specific image. The word 'jazzman' is funny on its own — it's a word no one under 60 uses, and Charlie using it with total confidence is peak character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: His goddamn heart just stopped for no reason.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Not no reason. You gave him a hot pepper.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't... They don't have to know that.

jokes.text: 'So I pranked him with a ghost pepper. You'd think that a jazzman would be more accustomed to spices, you know?'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains his rationale for the prank that caused a cardiac arrest
jokes.punchline: He genuinely believes jazz musicians have higher spice tolerance — a non-sequitur delivered with complete confidence as if it's common knowledge
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The logic is so specifically wrong that it feels like Dennis genuinely constructed this worldview. 'Jazzman' + 'accustomed to spices' is a non-sequitur that also reveals casual racism adjacent thinking that Dennis doesn't even register. It's dark, it's character-specific, it's quotable, and it's delivered as pure wisdom. Strong 8.

dialogue.line: You'd think that a jazzman would be more accustomed to spices, you know? Right? You'd think he'd be fine.

jokes.text: Frank receives his delivery burger in the middle of an active cardiac emergency and says 'It's about time'
jokes.setup: An ambulance is on scene, a man is dying on the floor, the gang is in crisis mode
jokes.punchline: Frank's only concern is that his Postmates delivery is finally here — delivered with zero acknowledgment of the emergency around him
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank. Two words that say everything about him. The setup is elaborate and his response is total indifference to human suffering. Economy score is very high — 'It's about time' in this context does enormous work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Sorry. Wh-What's with the food delivery here?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh. I'm, uh, doing a Postmates thing as a side gig.

jokes.text: Frank questioning why Dee is delivering food when she could just make him a smash burger in the apartment
jokes.setup: Dee is doing Postmates as a side gig; Frank ordered from her
jokes.punchline: Frank is oblivious to — or more likely indifferent to — the absurdity of making Dee bike across the city when she could just cook for him
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the ghost kitchen subplot. Frank's entitlement is on brand but the joke itself is mild — it's more infrastructure than punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You don't think I can make a burger and smash it? I'll smash a burger for you.

jokes.text: 'What the hell, Frank? A 5% tip? Pedal faster. It's cold as shit.'
jokes.setup: Dee just delivered Frank's food
jokes.punchline: Frank tipped 5% and is simultaneously insulting Dee's speed — total contempt stacked on contempt
jokes.explanation: Frank at his most casually cruel. The double insult — underpaying AND complaining about delivery speed — is very Frank. 'Pedal faster. It's cold as shit' has a good rhythm to it.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What the hell, Frank? A 5% tip?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Pedal faster. It's cold as shit.

jokes.text: What the hell, Frank? A 5% tip? / Pedal faster. It's cold as shit.
jokes.setup: Dee just rode her bike to deliver food to Frank
jokes.punchline: Frank's response to her complaint about a 5% tip is 'pedal faster' — no guilt, no apology, complete indifference to her suffering
jokes.explanation: 'Pedal faster. It's cold as shit.' is the kind of two-word demolition that Always Sunny does best. Frank's complete absence of empathy compressed into a delivery instruction. High economy score — it's four words and it's devastating. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Hey, did anybody else get, like, a crazy rush from that experience? I did. It's nice to have a little action around here, right?

jokes.text: 'That guy's gonna sue the shit out of me.'
jokes.setup: The gang watches the ambulance leave with the jazzman they poisoned
jokes.punchline: Frank's response to nearly killing a man is purely financial/legal self-interest, delivered as a matter-of-fact assessment
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank — no empathy, only liability. Functional but expected from the character at this point in the series.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You know, it's as close to playing God as you can get, you know? And the lifestyle. There's an appeal to it for sure.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis romanticize the EMT lifestyle — 'as close to playing God as you can get' — immediately pivoting from watching a man almost die
jokes.setup: A man almost just died because of them
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis are inspired not by guilt but by the aesthetic appeal of being EMTs — the lights, the sirens, the God complex, the sex
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — their motivation to become EMTs is entirely self-serving and superficial. 'As close to playing God as you can get' is a great line for Mac's God complex, and Dennis's 'the lifestyle is a vibe' is funny in its vapidity.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You know that they bang the doctors and the nurses, right?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Of course they do. Of course they do. Are you kidding me?

jokes.text: 'You know that they bang the doctors and the nurses, right?' / 'Of course they do. Of course they do. Are you kidding me?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are discussing the appeal of becoming EMTs
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts to the most base motivation — sex with hospital staff — and Mac validates it with absolute certainty
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis/Mac dynamic. Dennis's preoccupation with sex as a career perk and Mac's instant agreement is well-worn but executed cleanly. 'Are you kidding me?' lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The lifestyle is spicier than one of Frank's ghost peppers.

jokes.text: 'The lifestyle is spicier than one of Frank's ghost peppers.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is waxing poetic about the EMT lifestyle
jokes.punchline: He ropes in the ghost pepper incident — the very event that just hospitalized someone — as a positive metaphor
jokes.explanation: Early seed for the episode's spice motif. The callback is quick and the irony of using the pepper — which just hurt someone — as a positive comparison is on-theme. Mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You're not cake, are you?

dialogue.speaker: Jazzman
dialogue.line: Nah. It's just a joke between me and the guys...

jokes.text: Dennis approaches the jazzman in the hospital and asks 'You're not cake, are you?'
jokes.setup: Dennis visits the hospitalized jazzman, apparently to apologize
jokes.punchline: His opening question is whether the man might be a cake — a reference to internet 'is it cake?' videos — delivered with dead seriousness as a genuine concern
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Dennis visiting a comatose man he nearly killed and his opening concern being whether the man is secretly a cake is perfectly absurd and perfectly Dennis. The economy is flawless — four words do an enormous amount of work. The confidence of 'You never know with those guys' as a closing beat elevates it further. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, y-you know, actually, it's not my fault. Well, sure, I gave you a hot pepper and you had a heart attack, but, you know, I-I kind of attribute that to the... you know, the jazzman lifestyle more than the pepper.

jokes.text: Dennis begins to apologize to the comatose jazzman, then mid-sentence decides it's not his fault and blames the 'jazzman lifestyle'
jokes.setup: Dennis tells the unconscious man 'I came over here to say I'm sorry because...'
jokes.punchline: He catches himself, reverses, and blames the jazzman's lifestyle for his own cardiac reaction to being force-fed a ghost pepper
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dennis character work. The pivot mid-apology — 'Well, actually, it's not my fault' — is a masterclass in his narcissism. He builds the whole thing live in real time, landing on 'the jazzman lifestyle more than the pepper.' The callback to his earlier spice/jazz theory makes it richer on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Eh? Just checking about the cake thing. You never know with those guys.

jokes.text: 'Eh? Just checking about the cake thing. You never know with those guys.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered his non-apology to the comatose jazzman
jokes.punchline: He circles back to the cake concern as his closing thought — his primary takeaway from the hospital visit
jokes.explanation: The callback to the cake joke within the same scene works because it shows Dennis left the hospital with the cake concern unresolved, which is funnier than the initial joke. 'You never know with those guys' implies a whole world of cake-related paranoia.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What's with the getup?

dialogue.speaker: The Lawyer
dialogue.line: It's not a getup. It's an eye patch from when I was attacked by a bird.

jokes.text: The Lawyer appears wearing an eye patch — 'It's not a getup. It's an eye patch from when I was attacked by a bird.'
jokes.setup: Frank comments on The Lawyer's unusual appearance
jokes.punchline: The eye patch is from a bird attack — a callback to a previous season's events, delivered with wounded dignity
jokes.explanation: Good for fans of the show. The Lawyer's perpetual suffering at the gang's hands is a beloved running gag. The eye patch is a great visual and his defensive 'It's not a getup' is a solid straight-man line.

dialogue.speaker: The Lawyer
dialogue.line: Gruesome.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I wish I'd have seen that.

dialogue.speaker: The Lawyer
dialogue.line: You did see it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I don't remember.

jokes.text: 'Gruesome. I wish I'd have seen that.' / 'You did see it.' / 'I don't remember.'
jokes.setup: The Lawyer tells Frank he was present in court when a bird pecked out his eye
jokes.punchline: Frank says he doesn't remember witnessing this — either genuinely or as a legal tactic, and his initial reaction ('I wish I'd have seen that') is gleeful cruelty
jokes.explanation: Three-line exchange that's close to perfect in structure. 'Gruesome. I wish I'd have seen that' is Frank at his most delightfully sadistic. 'You did see it' / 'I don't remember' is a devastating two-beat. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: The Lawyer
dialogue.line: You don't remember being present in a court of law while a wild animal pecked out someone's eye?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Can you be more specific?

jokes.text: 'Can you be more specific?' — Frank's response to The Lawyer asking if he remembers being in court while a wild animal pecked out someone's eye
jokes.setup: The Lawyer asks Frank if he remembers witnessing the traumatic eye-pecking incident in a court of law
jokes.punchline: Frank asks for more specificity, implying this is not a unique enough event to narrow down
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The implication that Frank has witnessed enough courtroom eye-peckings that this one is insufficiently specific is a perfect capsule of his chaotic life. Three words doing maximum work. This is economy-of-comedy at a high level — earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm innocent.

dialogue.speaker: The Lawyer
dialogue.line: You literally just admitted it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I was lying.

dialogue.speaker: The Lawyer
dialogue.line: To a man in a coma?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I thought he was cake.

jokes.text: 'You just admitted to causing this man grievous harm.' / 'I'm innocent.' / 'You literally just admitted it.' / 'I was lying.' / 'To a man in a coma?' / 'I thought he was cake.'
jokes.setup: The Lawyer confronts Frank about his admission to the comatose jazzman
jokes.punchline: Frank's defense cascade: denial → 'I was lying' → 'to a man in a coma?' → 'I thought he was cake' — each beat more absurd than the last
jokes.explanation: The cake callback pays off brilliantly here. Frank using 'I thought he was cake' as a legal defense is exactly the kind of absurdist escalation this show does best. The structure is impeccable: each line of The Lawyer's indictment is met with a more indefensible Frank response, culminating in cake. This is the episode's funniest exchange and one of the stronger jokes in recent Sunny history.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, instead of taking 100% of the dose 10% of the time, we take 10% of the dose 100% of the time. That is scientifically more better.

jokes.text: 'I thought he was cake.' / 'Okay. I'll see you in court, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank needs to explain why he was lying to the comatose man
jokes.punchline: Frank's explanation — 'I thought he was cake' — so thoroughly baffles The Lawyer that he ends the conversation with professional resignation
jokes.explanation: The cake joke pays off beautifully here — 'I thought he was cake' as a courtroom defense is absurdist gold. The Lawyer's response of 'Okay. I'll see you in court, Frank.' captures exactly the right note of a man who has dealt with these people too long to even process it. The callback lands with maximum impact because it's the third deployment and the highest-stakes context. Highly quotable, perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The snugness, uh, really accentuates your physique. If-If that's okay to say. Uh... It's not, but let's continue, huh?

jokes.text: Mac's pepper microdosing theory: 'Instead of taking 100% of the dose 10% of the time, we take 10% of the dose 100% of the time. That is scientifically more better.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis want to get the benefits of hot peppers without the jazzman's fate
jokes.punchline: 'That is scientifically more better' — Mac delivers a mathematically correct but logically unsound breakdown with total confidence, capped by the grammatically broken 'more better'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Mac moment. The math sounds almost right, the logic is completely wrong, and 'scientifically more better' is a quotable closer that nails his pseudo-intellectual confidence. This seeds the macrodosing/blindness payoff perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: When I just referred to the gentleman to my right as my partner, I meant in medicine, not in life. In life, I am very much single.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis arrive at the EMT class clearly already affected by the peppers — sweating, agitated — and Mac compliments the instructor's 'snugness' of uniform
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are supposed to be taking a legitimate EMT certification class
jokes.punchline: They're visibly pepper-affected and Mac immediately hits on the instructor by praising how tight her uniform is
jokes.explanation: Cringe setup works — the instructor's patient exasperation vs. Mac's oblivious flirting. Mid-tier but functional. The 'if that's okay to say' hedge from Mac is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Now, when we get to the chest compressions, should I take your shirt off or should you take mine off?

dialogue.speaker: EMT Instructor
dialogue.line: No shirts come off.

jokes.text: 'When I just referred to the gentleman to my right as my partner, I meant in medicine, not in life. In life, I am very much single.'
jokes.setup: Mac called Dennis his 'partner' when explaining their enthusiasm to the instructor
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately clarifies he's single and not Dennis's life partner — unprompted clarification that reveals his anxiety about appearing gay (a long-running character dynamic) while also being a clumsy come-on to the instructor
jokes.explanation: Deep character work. Mac's internalized anxiety about his sexuality playing out as an unprompted, embarrassing over-clarification to a stranger is very well-observed. The 'in life, I am very much single' phrasing is awkward in exactly the right way. High character integration score justified.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, somebody doesn't understand double time. You see, I'm pushing to a much spicier song. Is everyone familiar with the Gipsy Kings's "Bamboléo"?

jokes.text: Mac confesses the peppers are affecting him mid-class: 'I think I got the dosage off. I think I ate a little bit too much. Less is more. That's on me.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are supposed to be professional students in a certification class
jokes.punchline: Mac is audibly suffering from pepper overdose and self-blaming in front of the class, treating his self-inflicted capsaicin poisoning with the gravity of a drug dosing error
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — the gap between their pretension (medical professionals) and reality (suffering from eating too many peppers) is the joke. 'That's on me' is a funny note of self-accountability in an otherwise unaccountable pair.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Say, "Yes, Chef." Why? Because the stakes are, uh, very high, you know, this is high-stakes stuff. Stakes of what? The cooking! It's-It's life-and-death stuff, man.

jokes.text: 'When we get to the chest compressions, should I take your shirt off or should you take mine off?' / 'No shirts come off.' / 'Actually, I'd love to take my shirt off. I'm getting pretty sweaty.'
jokes.setup: The class is about to begin CPR practice on dummies
jokes.punchline: Mac tries to make chest compressions into a shirtless scenario; the instructor shuts it down; Dennis pivots to wanting to take HIS shirt off due to pepper-sweating
jokes.explanation: Good layered joke — Mac's shirt removal is predatory/exhibitionist, then Dennis's shirt removal is a legitimate pepper symptom, which makes it funnier. The instructor's straight-man refusal grounds it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's a brick-based medium. Look at that. Yeah, that's my favorite part.

jokes.text: Mac takes over CPR compressions claiming he's 'increasing the rate to ensure maximum blood flow' and doing it 'to a much spicier song' — the Gipsy Kings' 'Bamboléo'
jokes.setup: CPR class is proceeding normally to 'Stayin' Alive'; Mac volunteers to demonstrate
jokes.punchline: Mac takes over and declares he's doing double-time compressions to 'Bamboléo,' framing dangerous CPR malpractice as a stylistic upgrade
jokes.explanation: Very good joke. The 'Stayin' Alive' BPM-for-CPR bit is a real thing, so Mac's upgrade to Bamboléo (a faster, more rhythmically complex song) is both absurd and weirdly internally consistent. 'Somebody doesn't understand double time' as a dismissal of the instructor is a great character beat — Mac's physical confidence overriding any concern about murdering the patient. 'Spicier song' ties it to the episode's motif perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That's because I got smashed by a Prius. Whoops! Yeah. I need some shin guards, I think.

jokes.text: Mac distributes peppers to the entire EMT class mid-CPR demonstration
jokes.setup: Mac has already commandeered the CPR demo and is doing it at double-speed to Bamboléo
jokes.punchline: He interrupts to offer peppers to classmates — escalating the chaos by dragging innocents into the microdosing scheme
jokes.explanation: Good escalation beat — the class is now fully derailed. The pepper distribution is funny as a pure 'what are you doing' moment.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You gotta say, "Yes, chef," "No, chef," "On your left, chef," "Corner, chef." These kind of things. It's gotta work that way, Dee.

jokes.text: 'Speaking of spice, I brought plenty of peppers for everyone.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just been riffing about 'spicy' rhythms for CPR
jokes.punchline: Mac has somehow brought peppers to EMT class and is now distributing them — taking the spice metaphor into literal territory mid-class
jokes.explanation: Solid escalation beat. The switch from metaphorical spice to literal pepper distribution in class is a good absurdist move. The implied visual of Mac passing out peppers during EMT training is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The illegality of what we're doing is spicy enough to get me off.

jokes.text: Maybe I should slip him a ghost pepper. / Yeah, well, that's a good idea.
jokes.setup: Frank is worried The Lawyer will sue him for the ghost pepper incident
jokes.punchline: His solution to the ghost-pepper lawsuit is to give The Lawyer a ghost pepper — the same crime he's being sued for — and Dee immediately endorses this plan
jokes.explanation: The circular logic of solving a ghost pepper lawsuit with another ghost pepper is very Always Sunny. The immediate endorsement from Dee is a good reaction beat — there's zero moral friction in this universe.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: This is Flaming Pepper, new truck on the rotation. We're only about a block away. We're gonna stop by.

jokes.text: 'What if he dies?' / 'Win-win either way, right?'
jokes.setup: Charlie asks what happens if the Lawyer dies from the ghost pepper
jokes.punchline: Frank considers the Lawyer's death a win-win with zero hesitation
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-line exchange. Charlie asking the obvious ethical question and Frank's immediate 'win-win either way' is Frank's whole worldview in four words. The economy is exceptional — this says everything about Frank without a single wasted syllable. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Now you're not microdosing anymore. You've slipped into macrodosing.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Macrodosing. That's cool 'cause it's my name.

jokes.text: I-I need the chili flakes, please. See them? / Yeah, I see 'em. / 'Yes, Chef.' / What? / Say, 'Yes, Chef.' / Why? / Because the stakes are, uh, very high, you know, this is high-stakes stuff. / Stakes of what? / The cooking! It's-It's life-and-death stuff, man.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Frank are cooking in the bar; Charlie demands professional kitchen protocol
jokes.punchline: Charlie insists on 'Yes, Chef' hierarchy for making a burger, and when asked why, escalates to 'it's life-and-death stuff' — the pomposity is completely divorced from the actual task
jokes.explanation: Charlie's kitchen ego is a great character beat. His insistence on 'Yes, Chef' in a bar kitchen, combined with 'it's life-and-death stuff, man' for burger preparation, is excellent character comedy. The escalation of stakes from chili flakes to existential gravity is well-constructed.

dialogue.line: Ma'am, you're gonna... you're gonna wanna keep that knee lukewarm. You're gonna wanna take short, shallow breaths.

jokes.text: Dee arrives with a smashed-up bike ('got smashed by a Prius') with shin guards and says it 'doesn't feel as bad' as it looks
jokes.setup: Dee is running her Postmates operation
jokes.punchline: She's been hit by a car and arrives mangled, but minimizes it — the shin guards were clearly insufficient
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the shin guards setup — she was clearly going to get hurt. 'Smashed by a Prius' and 'doesn't feel as bad' are both solid. Part of the ongoing Dee degradation arc.

dialogue.speaker: Patient
dialogue.line: Oh, my eye is burning.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Was there something on your thumb? It's probably unrelated.

jokes.text: 'Well, Charlie already made me one, so you get no tip.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just delivered Frank's smash burger while injured from being hit by a Prius
jokes.punchline: Frank refuses to tip because Charlie already made him one — no acknowledgment of her injury, no sympathy, just pure cheapness
jokes.explanation: Very Frank — the tip refusal after she's just been hit by a car is cruel in a way that's funny precisely because it's so casual. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You wanna pop that sweater off?

dialogue.speaker: Patient
dialogue.line: What? No, I need to rinse my eye.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, the sweater needs to come off.

jokes.text: Charlie's ghost kitchen demands: 'You gotta say Yes, chef / No, chef / On your left, chef / Corner, chef' — Dee initially refuses, then immediately complies when Frank starts to leave
jokes.setup: Charlie agrees to help Dee with her ghost kitchen operation
jokes.punchline: His condition is elaborate kitchen protocol language; Dee capitulates instantly when she realizes she needs him, then clearly doesn't care about the protocol at all once he's satisfied
jokes.explanation: Good Charlie bit. His insistence on kitchen hierarchy protocol in a dive bar is very Charlie Work energy. 'On your left, chef / corner, chef' are funny specifics. Dee's immediate capitulation is a good beat on her desperation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, let's make her unconscious.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Why?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I feel like this is becoming a whole thing.

jokes.text: Dee rides through traffic yelling 'On your left, bitch!' and 'Move it, boner!' — using the kitchen protocol language as road aggression
jokes.setup: Charlie demanded 'On your left, chef / corner, chef' as kitchen protocol; Dee agreed
jokes.punchline: She immediately repurposes the phrases as profane cycling aggression — 'On your left, BITCH'
jokes.explanation: Smart callback payoff. The kitchen phrase immediately becoming a profanity-laced cycling command is a good joke about Dee's character — she doesn't internalize rules, she just adapts them to her aggression. 'Move it, boner' is a great Dee line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: She definitely wants to bang me, dude.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, I think so.

jokes.text: 'The illegality of what we're doing is spicy enough to get me off.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are in a decommissioned ambulance they bought instead of taking the certification class
jokes.punchline: Dennis describes the illegality of the operation as sexually arousing — his pathological need for transgression framed as a pepper metaphor
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis — his arousal from danger and illegality is a core character trait and this line expresses it economically while tying to the episode's spice motif. 'Get me off' is appropriately transgressive.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Spice pot is spicy but needs more peppers. Peppers coming up. More peppers. I needed a "Yes, chef" there.

jokes.text: 'I mean, you take too much of those things and you can go temporarily blind.' / 'Blind? That's crazy. No, you can't.'
jokes.setup: Mac warns Dennis that too many hot peppers can cause temporary blindness
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly denies this — setting up his later blindness as a Chekhov's gun the audience can see coming while Dennis cannot
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural setup. Mac is correct, Dennis denies it, and the audience immediately knows Dennis is going to go blind. The dramatic irony is well-planted and the payoff is earned. Good rewatch value because you can see the whole arc from here.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't think he's gonna make it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Looks like he's gonna die.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Should we pepper?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You want some pepper, sir?

jokes.text: Mac claims taking too many hot peppers can make you temporarily blind — Dennis dismisses it, then immediately it becomes plot-relevant later
jokes.setup: Mac warns Dennis about temporary blindness from too many peppers
jokes.punchline: Dennis confidently dismisses it ('Blind? That's crazy. No, you can't.') — which the audience immediately knows will be proved wrong
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom plant — the audience knows this is coming back. Dennis's confident dismissal is structurally important setup. The rewatch value is high because knowing the payoff (Dennis does go blind later) makes this more of a dramatic irony beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Anything for my first responders. My guy. My guy. My guy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Getting high on your own supply over there?

jokes.text: The 'Flaming Pepper' vs 'Zebra 3' radio exchange — Mac and Dennis fake their EMT credentials on the official radio to take a call
jokes.setup: An official dispatch call comes through on the decommissioned ambulance's radio
jokes.punchline: Dennis deflects it as 'Zebra 3' saying they're 20 minutes out, then Mac countermands it as 'Flaming Pepper' — their ambulance's name — and takes the call anyway
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — from just sitting in an ambulance to actively impersonating EMTs on official dispatch. 'Flaming Pepper' as their truck name is funny, and the dispatcher just accepting it is a nice absurdist beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: A lot of blood in my line of work too.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, there shouldn't be.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, but you get the finger.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I got Frank once or twice.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis discover the injured woman on the sidewalk is Dee — knocked over by her own delivery bike after yelling 'on your left, bitch'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis respond to a 'turned knee' call; they don't know the patient
jokes.punchline: The patient is Dee, who they just saw, and she was apparently hit by her own delivery bike in the chaos from the previous scene
jokes.explanation: Good convergence of plots. The setup of Dee riding recklessly through traffic pays off when she becomes their emergency patient. The witness describing 'a crazy woman jumping the curb yelling nonsense about hot peppers' is a perfect encapsulation of Dee.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm sensing an opportunity to smash all of these ideas together... and really spice up our lives. Now I'm gonna float out something that I believe to be... a very reasonable proposition.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis pull each other aside to argue about whether Mac has 'macrodosed' the peppers — 'You've slipped into macrodosing.' / 'That's cool 'cause it's my name.'
jokes.setup: Dennis accuses Mac of eating too many peppers
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to 'macrodosing' is delight that it shares his name — his narcissism makes him miss the criticism entirely
jokes.explanation: Sharp joke. The wordplay (MAC-rodosing) is organic, not forced, and Mac's self-satisfied response perfectly captures his character. His ego is so large that a warning about his health is filtered through the lens of 'that word sounds like my name.' Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Popcorn ceiling, right next to the highway. This place is trash.

jokes.text: Mac quietly confronts Dennis: 'Did you pepper up?' / 'No.' / 'Yes, you did.' / 'No.' / 'Okay, I just had a little bit o...' / 'Goddamn it. Now you're not microdosing anymore. You've slipped into macrodosing.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis step away from the patient to confer
jokes.punchline: Dennis has overdosed on peppers, and Mac invents a new medical-sounding term — 'macrodosing' — to describe it
jokes.explanation: 'Macrodosing' is a good coinage — it's the natural antonym of microdosing, and Mac using it seriously as a medical diagnostic term is very funny. 'That's cool 'cause it's my name' is a nice additional touch — Mac taking personal pride in the word 'macro' because his name is Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh. Guess what, bozo? I don't care whether you eat it or not, but if you don't tip me, I'm taking out the other eye.

jokes.text: 'That's cool 'cause it's my name.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just coined the term 'macrodosing'
jokes.punchline: Mac notes with satisfaction that 'macro' contains his name — finding personal significance in a word he just invented
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfect character beat. Only Mac would derive personal pride from a prefix. The delivery timing is key — it's a slight non-sequitur that interrupts the medical seriousness. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Snake bite. That's kind of exciting. Whoa! That's very interesting to me. I've always wanted to suck out snake venom, you know this.

jokes.text: Uh, you're gonna... not wanna put anything hot on it. Or cold. / Yeah. Uh, nothing hot, nothing cold. / Yeah. Lukewarm, really. / Ma'am, you're gonna... you're gonna wanna keep that knee lukewarm.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are examining a woman with a possible sprained knee
jokes.punchline: Their combined medical advice eliminates both heat AND cold therapy, leaving 'lukewarm' — which is not a treatment — delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Very good joke about confident incompetence. The logical elimination of heat AND cold, arriving at 'lukewarm' as medical treatment, is both structurally sound and very funny. The confidence of the delivery ('you're gonna wanna keep that knee lukewarm') makes it land hard. Good Always Sunny fake-expertise joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dispatcher
dialogue.line: Got a possible code W59 in progress at Snyder and Pattison.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Pepper?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Pattison?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's like right here. Pepper? Pepper, anyone?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh! W59? What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Snake bite.

jokes.text: Mac rubs his pepper-contaminated thumb in Dee's eye during the 'concussion check' — 'Oh, God. My eye is burning. Was there something on your thumb?' / 'It's probably unrelated.'
jokes.setup: Mac wants to check Dee for a concussion and has her lay back while he examines her
jokes.punchline: His thumb, covered in ghost pepper residue, goes directly into her eye; his response to her burning pain is 'it's probably unrelated'
jokes.explanation: 'It's probably unrelated' is a great deflection line — it's the precise language of someone in denial about obvious causality, and it's very Mac. The setup (pepper-covered hands examining an eye) is well-constructed and the slapstick lands.

dialogue.speaker: The Lawyer
dialogue.line: What's in that?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That is 100% juiced Carolina Reaper tea.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I got him. Got him. Reaper tea.

jokes.text: 'Why don't I do some chest compressions on you. Wanna pop that sweater off?'
jokes.setup: Dee's eye is burning from Mac's pepper thumb; she's becoming hysterical
jokes.punchline: Dennis's solution is unnecessary chest compressions, with the sweater removal request revealing his actual motivation
jokes.explanation: Callback to the shirt-removal bit from the EMT class works. Dennis treating a sprained knee with chest compressions while asking for shirt removal is classic Dennis predatory behavior. Mid-tier but consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Bamboléo. Bamboléo. Bamboléo. Bamboléo. Bamboléo.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, let's make her unconscious.' / 'Why?' / 'I feel like this is becoming a whole thing.'
jokes.setup: Dee is panicking about her burning eye and demanding proper treatment
jokes.punchline: Mac suggests knocking Dee unconscious to solve the problem of her being difficult to treat; Dennis asks 'why' as if requiring a better reason
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest exchanges. Mac's solution to a difficult patient is to render her unconscious, and Dennis's 'Why?' doesn't object — it asks for clarification. 'I feel like this is becoming a whole thing' as the justification for assault is perfect. The casualness of their approach to patient harm is excellently captured here. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Goddamn it, Dennis. You have to yell "corner!" I can't see.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Goddamn it! I think I overdosed on the peppers.

jokes.text: 'Dude, this is incredible. I feel so alive.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have just provided terrible medical care, possibly injured their patient further, and are driving an unlicensed ambulance
jokes.punchline: Mac is experiencing pure joy — the contrast between the harm they're causing and his euphoria is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good irony — the worse they perform, the more alive they feel. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I swear there were other people there. I was strapped into a gurney. I passed out. Uh, they must have put me in an EMT uniform and-and-and fled the scene.

jokes.text: 'She definitely wants to bang me, dude.' / 'Yeah, I think so.'
jokes.setup: They've just subjected Dee (their friend/sister) to terrible medical care and Mac's pepper thumb in her eye
jokes.punchline: Dennis reads the situation as sexual interest from the victim; Mac agrees without hesitation
jokes.explanation: Dennis's inability to read a room, especially when it's his own sister, is well-worn but lands. His total confidence in this misread is character-specific.

jokes.text: Hey. Wow, he's okay. / Hey.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are transporting the patient to the hospital in their ambulance, apparently at high speed with chaos
jokes.punchline: The apparent discovery that someone survived (or is okay) is greeted with mild surprise — 'wow, he's okay' — as if survival was genuinely uncertain and also slightly disappointing
jokes.explanation: Brief reaction beat. Functions as a chaos interlude during the ambulance sequence. Thin joke on its own.

jokes.text: Move! / You dumb bitch. / Whoo. Yeah! All right.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are navigating their ambulance through city traffic
jokes.punchline: Their emergency driving consists of shouting 'you dumb bitch' at other drivers while expressing pure joy, contrasting wildly with the gravity of emergency services
jokes.explanation: Good energy beat. The disconnect between EMT gravity and 'you dumb bitch' as driving communication is well-calibrated but not especially inventive.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis do CPR on a patient in the ambulance while simultaneously yelling food orders at Charlie who is operating a ghost kitchen in the back
jokes.setup: The ghost kitchen and the fake EMT operations are now simultaneously happening in the same ambulance
jokes.punchline: Life-saving CPR and 'hot fries, stat' are indistinguishable in urgency — medical and culinary emergencies merged
jokes.explanation: The episode's central comedic convergence. The merger of the two subplots — ghost kitchen in an ambulance with CPR happening simultaneously — is exactly the kind of escalating chaos Always Sunny does best. 'Come on, Frank. Come on! Put the burger down. Go!' while doing CPR is a great line. The scene where medical and food urgency blur together is a strong structural payoff.

jokes.text: Real cardiac emergency: 'Should we pepper?' / 'You want some pepper, sir?'
jokes.setup: A man is going in and out of consciousness — a real medical emergency
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis's first instinct is to offer the dying man a pepper — their ghost pepper protocol applied to cardiac emergencies
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback — the episode opens with someone nearly dying from a pepper, and now Mac and Dennis are offering peppers as first aid to someone dying. 'You want some pepper, sir?' as emergency medical care is dark and absurd in equal measure. The circular logic of the episode is fully on display.

jokes.text: Come on. Come on. Come on. Come on. Come on. Let's go. / Go, go, go, go, go, go.
jokes.setup: The ghost kitchen operation in the bar is at full chaos, running like a real professional kitchen
jokes.punchline: The 'go go go' urgency for a ghost kitchen operation in a dive bar mirrors the ambulance urgency of the A-plot — the structural parallel is the joke
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure between ambulance chaos and kitchen chaos is a good thematic joke, but this specific moment is mostly setup energy rather than a payoff line.

jokes.text: 'Hot fries. Hot fries. Hot fries.' called out like a medical alert in the ambulance during CPR
jokes.setup: CPR is in progress on a patient in the ambulance
jokes.punchline: Charlie calling out 'hot fries' with the same urgency and rhythm as medical commands
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of 'hot fries' called with the cadence of a medical emergency is funny on its own. The repetition ('hot fries. hot fries. hot fries.') mirrors medical urgency perfectly.

jokes.text: 'Come on. Pick it up, grandpa.' — Mac to a patient during CPR
jokes.setup: Mac is performing CPR on what appears to be an elderly patient
jokes.punchline: He's heckling the patient for being slow to respond to resuscitation
jokes.explanation: Very dark and very funny. Heckling a dying person for taking too long to respond to CPR is a perfect Mac move — competitive and oblivious to basic human empathy. 'Pick it up, grandpa' is an excellent specific.

jokes.text: 'Whoo! Oh, God! It's all seeds. It's all seeds.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is in the ambulance doing CPR while apparently handling a pepper
jokes.punchline: He bites into a pepper that is 'all seeds' — the hottest part — and his reaction ('It's all seeds!') interrupts the CPR with equal horror
jokes.explanation: Good mid-chaos beat. The specific horror of 'it's all seeds' is relatable pepper-eating panic elevated by the fact that it's happening during active CPR. The exclamation has good energy.

jokes.text: Whoo! Oh, God! It's all seeds. It's all seeds.
jokes.setup: Mac is apparently biting into or handling a pepper during the CPR sequence
jokes.punchline: The discovery that the pepper is 'all seeds' — the hottest part — during an emergency medical situation, with the same dismay as a patient dying
jokes.explanation: Mac's horror at the seeds during CPR is a great comedic beat. The juxtaposition of man-dying and mac-seed-discovery as parallel crises of equal weight is very good. 'It's all seeds' is delivered with the gravity of a catastrophic diagnosis.

jokes.text: Frank abandons the ghost kitchen mid-rush to go trick the Lawyer — 'I gotta go trick The Lawyer' — Charlie left alone with a full kitchen rush
jokes.setup: The ghost kitchen in the ambulance is at full capacity with Charlie doing the cooking
jokes.punchline: Frank bails to execute his ghost-pepper-the-Lawyer scheme, leaving Charlie completely alone during the rush
jokes.explanation: Frank's self-interest abandoning Charlie is very on-brand. 'I gotta go trick The Lawyer' is a funny line in its matter-of-factness.

jokes.text: Oh, what? What? No. You can't go. Come on, I got orders, bud. / I gotta go trick The Lawyer. / Come on, I need my expediter.
jokes.setup: Frank tries to leave the ghost kitchen mid-service
jokes.punchline: Charlie's desperate plea retains kitchen vocabulary ('I need my expediter') while Frank's reason for leaving is to poison someone — the contrast between Charlie's professional commitment and Frank's murderous errand
jokes.explanation: Good juxtaposition. Charlie's professional kitchen dedication vs. Frank leaving to poison someone creates a funny tonal contrast. The 'expediter' vocabulary maintaining kitchen professionalism is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Mac's 'reasonable proposition' callback — 'I'm sensing an opportunity to smash all of these ideas together and really spice up our lives. Now I'm gonna float out something that I believe to be a very reasonable proposition.'
jokes.setup: Mac has had a sudden idea that merges the ghost kitchen, Dee's delivery service, and their ambulance operation
jokes.punchline: He delivers it in the exact same phrasing Dennis used at 02:26 — 'I'm sensing an opportunity... float something by you... very reasonable proposition' — a callback to the episode's cold open structure
jokes.explanation: Well-structured callback. The exact phrasing mirroring Dennis's earlier speech is a nice structural echo, implying they always approach schemes this way. 'Smash all these ideas together' is also a callback to the smash burger motif running through the Dee/Frank subplot.

jokes.text: Well, well, well. Hmm. New office, huh? / Popcorn ceiling, right next to the highway. This place is trash.
jokes.setup: The Lawyer arrives to meet Frank, now apparently in a makeshift office
jokes.punchline: The Lawyer's withering architectural critique ('popcorn ceiling, right next to the highway') is delivered as if he's a stern real estate appraiser rather than an opposing attorney
jokes.explanation: Good Lawyer character beat. The specificity of 'popcorn ceiling, right next to the highway' as a detailed insult suggests The Lawyer notices and catalogues ambient misery wherever the gang operates. Well-observed.

jokes.text: The Lawyer's first reaction to the ambulance-turned-office: 'Popcorn ceiling, right next to the highway. This place is trash.'
jokes.setup: The Lawyer arrives at the gang's new 'office' — apparently the ambulance or a space associated with it
jokes.punchline: His immediate assessment is contemptuous but accurate — popcorn ceiling by the highway is objectively awful real estate
jokes.explanation: Good Lawyer line — his perpetual disdain for the gang expressed through real-estate criticism. 'Popcorn ceiling' is a funny specific detail.

jokes.text: The Lawyer says he has terrible depth perception from 'the goddamn eye,' demonstrating it by misjudging distances
jokes.setup: The Lawyer is here to discuss a settlement
jokes.punchline: His eye injury is now functionally impairing his work and daily life — the ongoing consequences of the bird attack are still playing out
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff. The Lawyer's eye injury being a continuing functional impairment rather than just a cosmetic joke is a nice escalation of that bit.

jokes.text: Frank insists his chili is not poisoned, eats some himself to prove it, saying 'I promise' — it is clearly poisoned
jokes.setup: The Lawyer correctly suspects Frank's chili is poisoned and refuses to eat it
jokes.punchline: Frank protests it's fine and demonstrates by eating it himself — but the audience knows it's loaded with Carolina Reaper
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup — Frank eating the poisoned food to 'prove' it's safe. Functional, expected, but well-executed.

jokes.text: Let's talk about this like gentlemen. I brought you some chili. / Okay, I'm not eating that. I'm sure it's poison. / Besides, I ordered for myself. / No, my food's better. / And-And there's nothing the matter with that chili. That is tasty chili. / I-I promise.
jokes.setup: Frank tries to give The Lawyer his poisoned chili
jokes.punchline: The Lawyer correctly identifies that it's poison on first instinct, while Frank's protestations ('that is tasty chili, I promise') become more transparently guilty with each denial
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy payoff. The Lawyer's instant poison detection vs. Frank's increasingly pathetic 'it's just tasty chili, I promise' is a well-structured exchange. The Lawyer is smarter than everyone here, which is established by his suspicion being immediately correct.

jokes.text: Dee barges in to deliver food to The Lawyer and threatens: 'If you don't tip me, I'm taking out the other eye.'
jokes.setup: The Lawyer refuses food delivered by Dee
jokes.punchline: Dee threatens to remove his remaining eye if he doesn't tip her — escalating the tip dispute to eye violence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. It's a callback to the eye injury, a callback to the tip dispute, and an expression of Dee's barely-contained psychotic rage all in one. 'I'm taking out the other eye' as a Postmates tip threat is exactly the kind of line this show delivers. High quotability, earns near-8 on craft.

jokes.text: Dee eats The Lawyer's food because he won't tip her — 'If you're not gonna tip me, I'm eating your lunch' / 'Be my guest. I don't care.' — and it turns out to be Frank's poisoned chili
jokes.setup: Frank wants the Lawyer to eat the spiked chili; The Lawyer refuses; Dee eats it out of spite
jokes.punchline: Frank's scheme is foiled by Dee's pettiness — but Dee now gets poisoned, and The Lawyer inadvertently avoids the trap
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke. Dee's petty revenge (eating his food) accidentally triggers Frank's scheme against herself rather than the intended target. The Lawyer avoiding poisoning through pure indifference is a great beat. Well-structured dramatic irony.

jokes.text: Frank and The Lawyer both eating spiked food — Frank insisting 'it's the tiniest bit spicy' while clearly suffering
jokes.setup: Frank has eaten some of his own poisoned chili to prove it's safe
jokes.punchline: 'Not in temperature so much as it's the tiniest bit spicy' — Frank's massive understatement while presumably dying from Carolina Reaper exposure
jokes.explanation: Good understated delivery for a Frank moment. 'The tiniest bit spicy' while suffering from Carolina Reaper is good dramatic irony and self-incrimination rolled into one.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis respond to a 'W59 — snake bite' call that turns out to be fake — the gang faked a snake bite emergency to get them to come upstairs
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis excitedly take a W59 snake bite call; Mac declares he's 'always wanted to suck out snake venom'
jokes.punchline: The 'emergency' was manufactured by the gang to get the ambulance — there is no snake, they just needed help
jokes.explanation: Good structural convergence. 'I've always wanted to suck out snake venom, you know this' is a great Mac-specific detail — implying this is a known Mac desire. The fake emergency bringing all the plots together works well.

jokes.text: 'I've always wanted to suck out snake venom, you know this.'
jokes.setup: A snake bite call comes in
jokes.punchline: 'You know this' — Mac delivers this as an established fact about himself, as if Dennis is well aware of Mac's standing desire to suck out venom
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity of 'you know this' — implying this is a documented, repeated desire of Mac's — is perfect character comedy. It tells us everything about Mac: the fixation on physical contact under a heroic premise, the homoerotic subtext, the total confidence in this weird aspiration. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: The Lawyer toasts the chaos: 'I have absolutely no idea what the hell is going on here, but I guarantee you it's going to help me in my suit. I love watching all of you fail.'
jokes.setup: The whole gang is imploding simultaneously — Frank and Dee are suffering from hot chili, Mac and Dennis are fake EMTs
jokes.punchline: The Lawyer cheerfully acknowledges he doesn't understand the specifics but is delighted by the aggregate failure
jokes.explanation: One of the best Lawyer moments in the episode. 'I love watching all of you fail' is a pure expression of his earned schadenfreude and is very quotable. The structure — 'I have no idea what's happening but I know it helps me' — perfectly captures his relationship with this gang. Near-8 on craft.

jokes.text: Frank tricks The Lawyer into drinking '100% juiced Carolina Reaper tea' — 'I got you! Got him. Reaper tea. Somebody... What's happening to me?'
jokes.setup: Frank has been trying to poison the Lawyer throughout the episode; The Lawyer has been successfully avoiding Frank's traps
jokes.punchline: Frank finally gets him with Reaper tea disguised as regular tea — The Lawyer's confident 'I love watching you fail' is immediately followed by his own failure
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff. The Lawyer's toast celebrating the gang's failure is immediately followed by his own poisoning — the hubris punchline. 'What's happening to me?' echoes the jazzman's fate from the cold open, closing the loop thematically.

jokes.text: The Lawyer reacting to Reaper tea: 'Somebody... What's happening to me?'
jokes.setup: The Lawyer has just drunk Frank's Carolina Reaper tea
jokes.punchline: His quiet, confused deterioration — 'What's happening to me?' — plays against the chaos around him as a deadpan reaction beat
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat. 'What's happening to me?' is the right confused, almost philosophical note for the Reaper tea moment. Functional escalation.

jokes.text: Dennis goes blind mid-ambulance-operation: 'I can't see. Goddamn it! Goddamn you!'
jokes.setup: Mac warned Dennis at 10:20 that too many peppers cause temporary blindness; Dennis denied it
jokes.punchline: Dennis goes blind while operating an ambulance — the exact fate Mac predicted and Dennis dismissed
jokes.explanation: Well-earned payoff. The setup-and-denial structure (Mac warns, Dennis dismisses, Dennis goes blind) is textbook escalating irony. 'Goddamn you!' aimed at Mac for being right is perfect Dennis — he blames others for his own predictable mistakes. High structure score justified.

jokes.text: Mac yelling 'Corner!' while Dennis is blind and crashing the ambulance — callback to kitchen protocol as chaos ensues
jokes.setup: Dennis is blind, the ambulance is out of control, the Lawyer is poisoned, everyone is suffering
jokes.punchline: 'Goddamn it, Dennis. You have to yell corner!' — Mac's priority in the ambulance crash is kitchen protocol compliance
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The kitchen protocol language ('Corner!') returning at the moment of maximum chaos — blind driver, crashing ambulance — is a great structural joke. Mac's misplaced priority (protocol compliance during a crash) is perfect character comedy and the callback lands with full force because it's been seeded throughout the episode.

jokes.text: Judge delivers the verdict: 'Joyriding through the city, serving food without a permit in an unlicensed ambulance, all while impersonating medical professionals. For what? Your own twisted amusement?'
jokes.setup: The whole episode's plot gets summarized in one judicial sentence
jokes.punchline: The judge's incredulous 'For what? Your own twisted amusement?' — the actual answer is yes
jokes.explanation: Good summarizing joke — the judge's bafflement is a proxy for the audience processing what just happened. 'For your own twisted amusement' inadvertently being the correct answer is a nice structural note.

jokes.text: 'I swear there were other people there.' / 'I was strapped into a gurney. I passed out.' / 'They must have put me in an EMT uniform and fled the scene.'
jokes.setup: The gang is being sentenced
jokes.punchline: Three separate ridiculous defenses — each revealing the gang individually threw everyone else under the bus while trying to save themselves — culminating in Frank apparently being dressed in an EMT uniform by others
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific defenses. 'I was strapped to a gurney. I passed out.' is a great Dee line (passive victim framing despite being as culpable as anyone). Frank's 'they must have put me in an EMT uniform and fled' is delightfully absurd. Classic Always Sunny courtroom chaos.

jokes.text: Dennis's defense: 'Uh, they must have put me in an EMT uniform and-and-and fled the scene.'
jokes.setup: Dennis needs to explain why he was found in an EMT uniform
jokes.punchline: Dennis claims he was forcibly dressed in an EMT uniform by the others and abandoned — the least plausible explanation delivered with Dennis's characteristic confidence
jokes.explanation: Good closing joke. The specificity of 'they must have PUT ME in an EMT uniform' — the passive voice of victimhood — is a nice Dennis character note. His stammer ('and-and-and') suggests he's making this up in real time.

jokes.text: 'Thirty days, Philly Correctional. Next case.' — the judge's instant, dismissive sentencing
jokes.setup: Three increasingly absurd defenses have just been presented
jokes.punchline: The judge dismisses everything instantly with 'thirty days' and 'next case' — maximum contempt in minimum words
jokes.explanation: Good button on the episode. 'Next case' implies the judge has heard enough — the ultimate dismissal. Economy is very high for a closing beat.

tmdb_overview: After witnessing EMTs resuscitate a Paddy's patron, Mac and Dennis set out to become the pinnacle of masculinity; Frank tries to prove a prank's innocence with The Lawyer; Dee attempts to hack her part-time side hustle with Charlie's help as he descends into the fast-paced life of a chef.
